“The realm of divine dominion” is called “the divine realm” because it is close to God’s rule. There, the facts of existence prevail, while the mere possibilities of things fade into the background. — س ره

Logical division requires two distinct beings in every self-standing substance, as will become clear later. These philosophers deny that accidents, general kinds, or parts of a thing—such as legs or wings—have separate rulers of their own. — س ره

Their claim is like saying that a human being has a fixed side and a flowing side, or that place and quality each have fixed and changing sides. “Humanity” here means the shared nature that can be said of a human being, of what is fixed, and of what is flowing. “The First Adam” is the fixed human being spoken of in the words of our master and leader, Ali. — س ره

There are two reasons for the name. First, the rulers of kinds are images of what is above them, as God’s names and the forms of His names are. Second, they are models for the natural individuals below them. — س ره
The mind reaches these divine Forms when it understands general ideas. As explained earlier, understanding a general idea is like the soul seeing a luminous Form from a distance. — س ره

They believed that general knowledge and certain proofs aim at these Forms and reach them. General premises are about general things; individual cases are not learned through proof in the same way. These Forms and their states are lasting realities, reached through definitions, descriptions, and proofs. But people reach them to different degrees. — س ره
This does not mean an “abstract essence” in the technical sense, since no such essence exists, even in the mind. It means the nature considered without adding any condition. — س ره

The author is giving this interpretation the benefit of the doubt. At first, Avicenna explained the view as an essence considered apart from every feature, including oneness. Here he describes it as one, but only in the general sense, not as one individual. — س ره

On Avicenna’s reading, Plato would have thought that when philosophers say “humanity always exists,” they mean that one numerically identical human nature lasts forever. Avicenna says it means that humanity continues through successive people. A shared nature relates to its individuals as parents to children, not as one parent to all children: it exists through them, and its existence is their existence. — س ره

This later thinker’s argument is confused because it mixes up a shared nature and a general idea in the mind. Some of his claims fit the shared nature: considering it in itself and saying it of individuals. Other claims fit a mental idea: its being made into a distinct object of thought and stripped even of its abstractness. He says that if the general idea existed outside the mind, the features that make it an individual would be added to the essence from outside. That could apply to a shared nature, where individual features are analyzed as added; it does not fit a mental general idea. If he meant the mental idea, he should have concluded that it is not general but individual. The stronger reading is that he means a mental idea, made distinct by the mind, and then said of individuals because the general idea is the truth and the individuals are its lower-level forms. On this reading, his argument is different from Avicenna’s and comes close to Mulla Sadra’s point that understanding general ideas is like seeing Forms from a distance. But the argument does not establish that these Forms exist on their own. The author’s criticism is that the speaker seems to reach this conclusion by chance, without understanding it, and that his reasoning does not prove independent existence. — س ره

“The Intellects” means the separate Intellects. There is no difficulty in saying they are real beings: their contents are lasting, shared understandings. They are ways the Intellect itself exists. So it is more reasonable to say that they exist as originals, with individual things in nature as their shadows. — س ره
This objection is misplaced. These philosophers do not give accidents their own separate rulers. — س ره
This is a clear opening onto the subject. — س ره

A better reply is that natural kinds depend on higher principles and all are connected to God. The sensory world is where the luminous Forms appear, like the broad base of a cone of light; it is not the point where all that light is gathered into its simplest and highest form. Everything the author says about the lasting existence of things in the timeless order, and their freedom there from the limits of matter, can be accepted. But in that respect, these things are the display and many-sided appearance of the luminous Forms, not the Forms in their highest, most unified state. The Forms also have a higher state, where they are beyond separation and gathered together, and where the many are held within the one. Material things depend on God even in the timeless order. Still, the existence of particular material things is at the lower level of that timeless order, while the luminous Forms exist at its higher levels. As for the author’s objection that material individuals have many separate existences, the teacher he quotes says they are one insofar as they are related to the one source. The wise have compared times and timed events to a point, and places and things in places to a point, when compared with higher principles. — س ره

This objection applies to the first two arguments. Followers of Aristotle need not deny that changes in matter depend on a separate intellect. But a separate intellect relates equally to all such changes. To bring about a particular change, something must determine which one occurs. If that determiner is also separate, the same problem returns. So there must be a material determiner for each particular event, working together with the separate intellect. The argument establishes no more than this. — ط مد
The earliest philosophers treated what exists in a bearer and an accident as the same. That is why they called the forms of natural kinds dependent features. — س ره

This is questionable. The fact that a thing can exist without a power does not make the power an accident. An accident is something that exists in a bearer that can exist without it both as a being and as a kind. Aristotle’s followers call the forms of natural kinds substances. Avicenna defines a substance as something that exists in no other thing in this way: it is not a part of that other thing and cannot be separated from it. — س ره
What preserves and maintains the body is the power that continues through time. It cannot remain all at once; it lasts through an unbroken sequence, and its effect lasts in the same way. — س ره
This phrase either connects to the point just made or gives the reason that comes before the claim it explains. It introduces the explanation beginning “These different actions.” — س ره

I would say the growth power does not make a painful break. A break in continuity causes pain. Instead, it produces one small amount of growth, then another, in a continuous increase. Just as the added amounts join to form one continuous quantity, each stage of growth follows continuously from the one before it. The process does not involve separate movements in different directions. — س ره

There is no need to deny the existence of powers within bodies or of natural forces in order to establish separate governing intellects. The powers in bodies can be channels through which separate causes act; those higher causes are too noble to perform each limited physical act directly. The powers within bodies are placed under them, and all are under the Creator of powers and abilities. Also, remarkable actions do not always require knowledge or awareness of their causes. Look at the honeycomb’s hexagons, the spider’s triangular webs, or nature’s conical flames and round droplets, bubbles, and foam. — س ره

If the author means that we lack a full, connected understanding of these processes, I agree—but such understanding is not required. If he means that we have no awareness of them at all, even a simple, direct awareness, that is not right. He himself later affirms that the soul has direct awareness of its powers and actions in the discussion of divine knowledge. — س ره

Granted, these powers are not made of parts. But why could they not have different levels, like light, which has one simple reality yet varies in completeness? One level is the most intense light; another is the light of the sun and moon. The governing light has one level in which it acts willingly, another in which it acts by choice, and another in which it acts by nature. Yet it remains one simple light, whose unity is real but dependent, like a shadow. As the Persian verse says: “How the shadow draws the forms of saints— / a sign pointing to the light of God’s sun.” — س ره

That is, the kinds would have ceased to remain stable, and then something other than a human might have come from a human, and so on. Since the kinds do not cease or change, they must have rulers and Forms that are their principles and ends. Their stability does not mean that they have no beginning or no end. The argument also leaves out another premise: the kinds are many and distinct, while God is one in every respect, so their differences cannot result from depending on God directly, without intermediaries. But this is open to question. If they depend on distinct aspects of the Active Intellect, as Aristotle’s followers say, then they need not be alike. The author’s stronger point is not only that the kinds have causes and ends, but that they share the same kind as their Forms. He argues that if the form of a kind were not based on a luminous model, it would be like an individual form produced by chance from matter and its features. There would be no order or stability; in the world of motion and chance, it might not appear at all. Since the human form, for example, is preserved, it must have an eternal model in the creative world. The bodily form is its shadow, and the two are alike in kind. This differs from saying that bodily kinds depend on aspects of the Active Intellect, such as possibility and necessity, or its knowledge of itself and of near and distant principles. These are clearly not of the same kind as particular creatures. — س ره

There is no problem in leaving the exact cause unidentified. The soul does not gain completeness by knowing these individual details. It is enough that each body has a particular mixture and readiness to receive a certain color, along with the way light enters and blends. — س ره

The image and its ruler each serve as a model for the other, though the word “model” is more often used for the ruler. Here it refers to the ruler. You might ask how their view leads to an endless chain of models. Suhrawardi explains this in The Wisdom of Illumination: a particular form cannot exist without a meaning. If the image that serves as ruler is itself a particular form, it must have another model, and so on. Here, the author uses “mold” to mean something like a body for a spirit. Later, when he says that the rulers of kinds were not made by the First Creator to be models and molds for what lies below them, he means models in the sense of a design or plan. — س ره

That is, “universal” in the sense that the outpouring of life reaches all individuals equally, not a concept that can be said of many. In The Wisdom of Illumination, the ruler is called universal because its care reaches all these individuals equally. It is the universal and the original, but not a shared concept. — س ره

The proof given so far establishes only that a nobler level of existence must be real if a lower one exists. It does not prove that both levels belong to the same kind. Material kinds call for, or point to, earlier immaterial beings that match them in perfection. But that does not show that each immaterial being is a model of the same kind as the material things that match it. The author sees this problem too: after giving three arguments, he says they do not prove that an intellectual Form belongs to the same kind as its bodily image. The fact that one being has the perfection of another does not mean they share its kind. Higher Intellects contain the perfections of material kinds, yet differ from them in nature. God contains all perfections but has no essence of his own.

Mulla Sadra also says in other places that the same concept can have different forms of existence in different things. Knowledge, for example, is a quality in the human mind; the soul’s direct knowledge of itself is a soul-substance; the Intellect’s knowledge of itself is an intellectual substance; and God’s knowledge of Himself is identical with His existence, which has no essence. The concept is the same in each case, but its reality differs. — ط مد
The proof is also given in the metaphysics section of this work. — س ره

That is, if a lower being came into existence after it was already possible in itself. This is what the author means by saying “How could it be otherwise?” and pointing to the marvelous order. The reasoning is not circular. — س ره

They do not claim that accidents have separate rulers of their own. If they did, an accident would not belong to a subject, and the subject would need a capacity to receive it. This would mean there was potentiality and matter in the creative world, and the accident would become a self-subsisting substance—like a scent existing on its own. That follows only if the Forms are exact counterparts. If they are images only in the looser sense of correspondence, then, as the Illuminationist master says, there can be luminous intellectual forms corresponding to these qualities, such as love and pleasure. — س ره

The third proof, based on the possibility of a nobler being, is meant to establish that Forms and their images share one nature. Those who accept this principle usually require the higher and lower beings to have the same essence. Otherwise, if they were different kinds, someone could say that the higher kind did not exist before the lower because it was impossible. This follows from the fact that possibility, necessity, and impossibility belong to an essence: if one individual of a kind is possible, then all are possible; if one is necessary, all are; and if one is impossible, all are. The author reports this condition in the metaphysics section of this work. He has also used sameness of kind in his earlier argument against chance: wheat does not come from barley.

The author himself noticed the difficulty. After presenting the three proofs, he says they do not establish that an intellectual Form belongs to the same kind as its image. The fact that a perfection found in one essence exists in another being does not make that other being part of the same kind. Higher Intellects contain the perfections of material kinds, but differ from them in essence. God contains every perfection and has no essence. — س ره
They name the ruler of a kind after that kind, with “Yazad” as another name for Haoma, not as a word of possession. — س ره
Suhrawardi means to deny that these rulers are material, or have features that depend on matter. He does not deny that they resemble their images. — س ره

This is a stronger objection than the first. It asks how, even on Suhrawardi’s account of images, a simple luminous essence could represent an animal whose legs and wings are parts of its nature. The objection can be answered only by Mulla Sadra’s principles: existence is primary, its degrees differ, and substance itself can change. — س ره
That is, “either bodies or dark forms.” The word “or” here divides a whole into its parts; it does not divide a general concept into separate kinds. — س ره

These lights belong to a level whose members are equal in rank; unlike the higher, ordered levels of Intellects, there is no chain of causes and effects among them. The main objection is that Suhrawardi’s view of the rulers of kinds conflicts with his view that essence, not existence, is primary. If the worlds and their models correspond, their differences should be differences of degree—greater or lesser light—not differences of kind. That would fit the view that existence is primary: the same reality of existence would be present in the bodily images at different levels, while the differences in kind would come from differences in the levels of existence. But then the worlds and their images would not correspond in the way described, or the view that all lights are degrees of one reality would have to be abandoned. In The Witnesses, Suhrawardi says that all Intellects are one kind, and that they cannot be true individual members of many different natures. — س ره

This goes further than the point made earlier. Earlier, the author seemed to treat everything except the final distinguishing feature as a true part of the kind. Here he points to what he established before: what makes a kind what it is, in the fullest sense, is its final distinguishing feature and its source; the rest are conditions and tools. The true forms of bodily kinds, as images of their rulers, are therefore their final distinguishing features and simple forms. Even in a natural human being, matter, bodily form, growth, and sensation through separate organs are not what ultimately define the kind. — س ره

Mental images play opposite roles in the two comparisons. As features that depend on the mind, they are compared first to forms that exist in matter. As images free of matter in the intellect, they are compared later to the separate Forms in the creative world. — س ره

This claim does not fit the stature of Aristotle, the First Teacher, through whom and others like him the lights of true knowledge spread. A report even says that he was a prophet, though people of his time did not recognize him. The rulers who spent time with him, such as Alexander, were among the better kings and leaders. — س ره
This is the life of existence that flows through all things, not life in the sense of awareness and action, as when we say that a living thing perceives and acts. — س ره
This is praise phrased to sound like criticism, like the saying, “I am the most eloquent of people, yet I am from Quraysh.” — س ره

This is the basis of the reply: the First Creator is simple in reality and contains all things in a higher way, with true and complete unity. The higher world flows from Him and contains all things as shadows, with a unity that is real but dependent. — س ره

“Words” in the teacher’s phrase “words of the Teacher” means active principles, whether separate from matter or joined to it. This includes the Forms of kinds. The author often uses “words” to mean existences. This use also agrees with sacred books and the sayings of the Imams: Jesus is called a Word; the Qur'an says, “If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord”; and a saying calls the Imams “the complete Words.” A word expresses what is within; existences express what is hidden in the unseen; and active powers express the all-encompassing power. — س ره

The soul reaches its full development by traveling through the lands of general realities and swimming in their seas. A general reality includes all its endlessly many particulars, and the soul can grasp that general reality. Particular things are only flashes from it. Knowing them does not complete the soul or give it any lasting gain. The restless soul values them only because it is tied to the body. For example, a particular fruit may appeal to you because of the heat of your liver; without that bodily condition, you would not seek it, and it would have no special appeal. Do not become attached to things that seem beautiful only because of the body and its powers. The words “although each is particular” form an exception that sounds like criticism but is meant as praise. — س ره
That is, the plant in the world of imagination, where it has size and shape. — س ره

A similar relation appears among the higher Intellects and in the hearts of people of knowledge and insight: their beliefs and direction are one. The perfected ones, from Adam to the Seal of the Prophets, share one reality. As the saying goes, “The souls of God’s lions are united,” and “the believer is a mirror to the believer.” Each sees himself and all things in the other. — س ره

In this short summary, the author does not repeat the earlier interpretations of Plato’s Forms because he considers them far-fetched. If he meant an essence without any qualification, that would return to Avicenna’s interpretation and be just as far-fetched. If he meant a general idea in the mind, that would return to the interpretation the author gives here. — س ره

This is another proof for the existence of intellectual Forms, beyond the three already given by the Illuminationist philosopher. The general ideas we understand must exist somewhere. They either exist on their own or in something else. If they exist in something else, they must be in a part of our material body, in our soul, or in a separate intellect. The argument rules out these alternatives, leaving Forms that exist on their own. Since they correspond to bodily kinds, each would then be a distinct, nonphysical individual of that kind.

But there is another possibility: one immaterial being could contain all the qualities and capacities of the material world, while the Forms seem different because of the way we perceive it. By sensing different individuals, the mind becomes ready to connect with this intellectual being and know it directly. Our readiness makes the one being appear to us under different concepts. This is like how we form ideas of knowledge, power, life, hearing, and sight by noticing different qualities in ourselves, then attribute each idea to God. His reality is one, with no separate attributes. The concepts differ because our understanding changes, not because His reality is divided.

The same could be true of human, horse, sheep, and other Forms: we connect with one intellectual reality that contains all the qualities and capacities found in the material world. This does not mean one undivided being contains several different natures. Instead, we form each general idea by relating that being to the material individual we have perceived. — ط مد

The same problems raised earlier about things existing in the mind arise here too. A form would have to count both as a thing in its own right and as a feature of something else, among other conflicts. In short, those problems remain whether the forms are said to exist in the soul or in a separate intellect. — س ره

These problems arise whether the forms exist in a separate Intellect, as Aristotle’s followers say, or on their own, as the author holds. Either way, many forms would come from one undivided source, or exist within God’s own being. If someone answers that the separate Intellect has many aspects—such as its acts of illuminating, knowing, loving, and ruling—those aspects could explain the forms. But then the forms would be that Intellect’s knowledge of its own principles. They could not come before its own active powers, so they would not be separate causes producing many forms within it. If someone says the forms exist there in a chain of causes and effects, as Aristotle’s followers do, the Illuminationists reject this because many of the forms stand at the same level. — س ره

In the author’s view, forms that exist on their own are general in the same way that forms in the intellect are general in Aristotle’s school. This does not mean there are two sets of forms, as some theologians claim when they distinguish between forms existing “in” the mind and forms existing “through” it. — س ره
As the saying goes, “Whoever loses a sense loses the knowledge it brings.” — س ره
If we draw a straight line of limited length, fix one end, and turn the other end until it returns to its starting point, we make a true circle. Many shapes have been proved in this way. — س ره

The assumption is that the material and separate cases share the same nature. If the material cases could not exist without an added feature, then the separate cases could not exist without it either; both would depend on that feature. Or the point may be that if an added feature makes a cause necessary, that cause must still exist before the thing that bears the feature, since an effect depends on its cause by its very nature. — س ره

I would say the reverse. There is a great difference between human nature as it exists in the divine realm, where it is at once knowing, knowledge, and known, and the same nature as it exists in bodily life. There is also a great difference between the powers that cause kinds to exist—such as necessity, possibility, and essence, whether considered alone or together with spatial position—and the complete patterns of those kinds. The higher natures are understood as they exist in a world where all things are joined, not as bare concepts or outlines. — س ره

The earlier reply shows that Avicenna’s argument fails for natures whose instances differ in degree, a distinction everyone accepts. Here the answer goes further, using the Illuminationist view that a nature itself can vary in degree: its level is both what differs and what makes the difference. Avicenna’s argument would work if every instance of a nature had the same level, like one fixed shade of white. It does not work if the nature can be stronger or weaker, like the difference between the whiteness of ivory and straw. — س ره

First, being limited or unlimited usually applies to quantities. Here the author has assumed that an image in the world of imagination is separate from matter, like an intellect. One might answer that it is still an extended image, so it can be limited or unlimited in its size, though not by its nature as an immaterial being. Second, if Avicenna’s argument worked, it would also rule out extended images in the world of imagination. But the Illuminationists say such images exist apart from ordinary matter. They also allow there to be endlessly many of them. The proof against infinite quantities does not apply to these images: they are not moving bodies or parts of one continuous, infinitely long space. They are simply unlimited in number, with no order or chain of causes among them. — س ره

This conflicts with what the philosophers—and the author himself elsewhere—say: only God and His complete Words exist before time. Perhaps the author means that each part of time comes into being anew, with nonexistence before and after it, even though God’s giving of existence never stops. — س ره

This is especially true of the borrowed beloved who is a fully perfected human being. The way this image is real is that we see it only as something that disappears into the One who appears through it—like wine without a cup. This may be why the Prophet said, “I was made to love three things from your world.” The soul’s turn toward the true Beloved is real in truth, even if it outwardly seems to be drawn to an image. Few people see the sun in water and recognize the sun itself without being distracted by the water. — س ره
The veils of light are realities that exist apart from bodies, such as intellects and souls. The dark veils are bodily things. The number points to a meaning discussed elsewhere. — س ره
Rumi puts it well: “If this is your fire, what must your light be? If this is your grief, what must your form be?” — س ره

This describes an individual image held in the imagination. What, then, of someone whose whole attention—or most of it—is fixed on general truths and whose aim rises above passing particulars? How far apart are understanding something through the intellect and picturing it in the imagination; how far apart are their kinds of lasting life. — س ره

The images we sense also have no lasting faithfulness or stability. Intellectual forms, by contrast, remain without change. They are like the meaning behind the world’s many appearances, or like the preserved root of a tree in its branches. Their change is like the changing appearance of a person’s body, while the person’s identity remains. When this lasting reality becomes a form for the soul, and the soul receives it as its matter, the soul is completed by that form and gains its lasting, self-sufficient life. — س ره

The commentator sees two readings of “identity” here. It may mean unity in general, whose kinds include predication, sameness in kind, and related forms. Or it may mean predication, divided into what applies in itself and what applies incidentally. It does not mean the other familiar divisions of predication into primary and common, direct and derivative forms; those are not investigated here. The first reading is supported by the author’s detailed discussion of sameness in kind later on and his lack of a detailed discussion of types of predication. The second is supported by his listing sameness in kind and related forms alongside identity here. — س ره

This names a specific kind after a general one. Two things that differ either share a nature—in which case they are alike—or they do not. If they do not, they may still be able to exist together in the same thing; then they are merely different. If they cannot exist together in that way, they are opposites. — س ره
The word “collection” directly means a gathering, and the word “units” implies a group. A group is an example of the general idea of gathering, which is the same idea as multiplicity. — س ره

This is a reminder, not a definition. A definition explains a general idea grasped by reason, not a particular thing sensed or pictured in the imagination. Nor is saying what something is not a definition: we already know that every thing is not every other thing. For example, we can define a human as a rational animal through a general idea, then draw attention to that idea by pointing to a particular person, such as Zayd. — س ره

This divides a thing into categories that can overlap. “One insofar as one,” which is the same as unity itself, is also genuine unity. Later, the author uses “genuine unity” in a broader sense. — س ره

That is, it is not a settled feature that remains in its subject. It may still be a feature that does not stay fixed, such as facing or touching. The philosophers also say that division can result from two features, whether these remain fixed or not. — س ره

The thing made up of several things is “one by kind”; this does not mean that the general kind itself is the basis of unity. The example of a human being and a horse makes this clear: “animal” is one general kind, while humans and horses are one by kind. The same applies to the other examples. — س ره

Humanity is the shared feature of a writer and a person who laughs. It is outside their definitions, yet can be said of both. In the technical use here, an attribute is something said of a subject but not part of what the subject is. Humanity is an attribute of being a writer or a laugher in this sense. — س ره
Some copies of the metaphysics section of The Healing read kasīr here, with an unpointed sīn. — س ره
“As a whole” refers to the celestial sphere. Being divided in two ways means being divided into individuals of a general kind and being divided into matter and form. — س ره
Unlike celestial bodies, sizes can be divided into individual examples but not into matter and form, because quantities are simple in the outside world. — س ره
The fact that one occurs in every number is also an example of creation disappearing into God in the Great Resurrection. — س ره

Numbers are repetitions of unity. Repeating something is a way for it to appear; if its appearance were separate from it, it would be another thing, not its appearance. Each number is made of repeated ones and has no form beyond them: two is one and one; three is one and one and one; and so on. This is true of numbers as signs. Created beings, by contrast, have their own distinct parts: a house is made of a roof and walls, not a roof and another roof. Although unity is the basis of every number, the numbers themselves have different natures, qualities, and effects. Any two different numbers are entirely distinct: two is not three, and three is not two. Among examples such as the ocean and its waves, a moving flame, a circle, and different kinds of motion, the relation between unity and number is the clearest example of divine oneness. Perhaps this is why Zayn al-Abidin prayed, “My God, the oneness of number belongs to You.” — س ره
Al-Kafi says, “We have states with God: we are He, and He is us.” It also says, “He is within things, but not by mixing with them.” — ن ره

The identity of unity and individual identity follows from the identity of unity and real existence, since the author has already said that being an individual thing is real existence. The author raises this objection and reply as he turns to unity and identity. The next objection concerns unity being the same as real existence. — س ره

The mistake may be that the objection treats a feature of a thing as part of what the thing is. The identity that remains is the identity of the underlying matter, just as its vague unity remains. The unity of continuity disappears, and so does the identity of that continuity. Or the mistake may come from using “body” in two senses: the extended form that first appears to us to be the body, and the body as matter together with form. The identity of the first disappears; the second remains. — س ره

The earlier principles show that existence in general divides into one and many, and that the many exists just as the one does. Yet every thing is one insofar as it exists. So existence in general always goes with unity in general. When we compare one existent thing with another, however, we can divide them into one and many. The author is discussing this particular kind of unity, which is opposed to multiplicity. Its opposite, multiplicity, exists, though it is not itself one. This is like other divisions of existence in general: into actual and potential, or into things outside the mind that have effects and things that exist only in the mind. Existence applies to both sides, and being actual applies to all that exists outside the mind. The reason is that existence has different degrees: strong and weak, pure and mixed. Features such as unity and actuality apply to all these degrees, but when we compare them, the weaker lacks what the stronger has. Avicenna’s argument therefore proves that particular unity differs from existence, but it does not show that unity in general differs from existence. — ط مد
This rejects the first claim in the argument. — س ره
That is, if we exclude unity in general. But multiplicity, when opposed to a particular kind of unity, exists; it is one of the two divisions of existence in general. — ط مد

This is not a third option, since the argument gave only two. It chooses the second: multiplicity exists in reality, not only in the mind. The disagreement is about how the word “many” applies. The reply treats multiplicity as a feature that can coexist with unity in the underlying thing. The objection instead makes being many part of the thing itself. — س ره
Here “sameness” means ordinary predication—saying one thing of another—not a definition in which the subject and predicate mean the same thing. — س ره

The commentator is referring to the philosophers’ claim that a shared existence is the main basis for saying one thing of another. They do not mean that predication is the same as judging a statement to be true. A conditional statement, for example, has an “if” part and a “then” part, and the shared existence described here does not make either part a judgment by itself.

Nor do they mean that shared existence is the only thing needed. Possibility and human nature share an existence; on the accepted view, so do blackness and a body. Yet we do not say “a human is possibility” or “a body is blackness.” We need a link that makes the feature belong to the subject. English shows this link in words such as “possible” and “black.”

To understand this, we need two distinctions. Something can exist in itself, like a body, or exist as a feature of something else, like blackness in a body. It can also exist for itself or for another. Two natures cannot be joined in every respect, because then they would be one thing, not two. They must differ in one respect and be joined in another. Their difference lies in what each is in itself; their unity lies in one being a feature of the other.

Take a body and blackness. They share one existence, but the body exists in itself while blackness exists as a feature of the body. The predicate “black” says that the body has that feature. In this way, blackness removes from the body the lack of being black. This is what logicians mean when they say that a statement has two parts: one identifies the thing we are talking about, and the other says what feature belongs to it. At heart, a statement has a subject, a predicate, and a judgment. Any separate link between them belongs to the predicate, not to a fourth part of the statement.

From this we can see that, in philosophical terms, a statement joins something that exists in itself—the subject—to a feature that exists in it—the predicate. The familiar formula “same in existence, different in meaning” is not quite exact. More precisely, the subject and predicate differ in the way each exists in itself, and they are joined because the predicate exists as a feature of the subject.

Predication takes different forms according to how the feature belongs to its subject. One form is when a thing is related to itself in the mind, as when we say “a human is a human.” This is an essential definition. Another form joins two levels that differ in completeness, such as a thing and the causes on which it depends. This is called predication between a higher reality and its lower reflection. A third form links a feature to the thing it belongs to, as when we say “the body is black.” This is ordinary predication. Finally, sameness in this sense is not limited to ideas in the mind. A statement that includes a judgment exists in the mind, but the relation between things described here can also hold outside it. — ط مد

This is only a possible view, not one known to have been held. One might suppose that Democritus’s tiny, hard bodies—the basic parts from which he thought larger bodies were made—differed in kind and therefore differed in how they join and separate. But Democritus himself did not hold this view. — س ره

A definition must match what it defines. Also, if shared existence alone were enough for ordinary predication, an effect could not differ from its cause, since an effect cannot exist without its cause. So this is not a mistaken reversal of the definition. — س ره

The point is that saying one thing of another requires both some unity and some difference. Things may share a kind, a quality, or another feature, but that alone does not make predication possible. The conjunction here means “even though both are present,” not that the passage has moved to a separate point. — س ره

This challenges the scholar who says that ordinary language restricts predication to shared existence. He says that resemblance and related forms of unity cannot support predication because their shared feature is a common nature, not existence. The commentator replies that a shared nature can also support sameness. He then asks how someone who treats a thing’s nature as primary can also say that identity is the same as existence. If “existence” means only that the nature is related to its maker, that relation alone does not make the thing an individual. — س ره

In an earlier note, the commentator said this point applies to things made of separate parts, but not to simple things. Color, for example, is not a separate thing within whiteness. A better account is that essential parts, such as animal nature and rational nature, differ in what they are; that is why we can divide a definition into a general kind and a distinguishing feature. Parts of a measured length, by contrast, share the same nature. Cutting them apart is not the same kind of division. This is why a measured part differs from its whole more fully than two things that share a definition. — س ره
